q: If a LangGraph graph has only linear edges (`A → B → C → END`), it's expressible as a chain. What does LangGraph buy you over a LangChain chain when the graph *is* genuinely branching?
answer_outline: Three things a chain doesn't give you cleanly. (1) Conditional routing — `add_conditional_edges` decides the next node based on state at runtime. In a chain you'd use `RunnableBranch`, but the branching logic gets buried in a Runnable composition rather than expressed as a graph topology you can see. (2) Parallel fan-out with state convergence — two nodes write to the same field via a reducer, both run concurrently, downstream nodes wait at the implicit barrier. `RunnableParallel` does this for output dicts but doesn't compose with conditional routing as cleanly. (3) Per-node state diff streaming via `graph.stream(updates)` — you see exactly which node fired and what it changed. Chains give you final output or per-step output via callbacks, but not the same node-shaped granularity. The cost is more ceremony for simple flows; pay only when the flow is actually graph-shaped.

q: Two parallel nodes write to the same field in `state`. Without a reducer, what happens, and what does adding `Annotated[list[T], operator.add]` change?
answer_outline: Without a reducer, LangGraph raises `InvalidUpdateError` because it doesn't know how to merge concurrent writes — last-write-wins isn't safe when both writes are concurrent. Adding `Annotated[list[T], operator.add]` declares a reducer (here, list concatenation) so LangGraph knows: when multiple nodes return updates to this field in the same step, append them. Other reducers exist (e.g. `operator.or_` for sets, `dict.update`-style for dicts, custom functions). The pattern generalizes — anywhere parallel writes exist, you must declare how to merge them. It's the same shape as the `applicative` / `monoid` discipline if that vocabulary helps; here it's just 'tell me how to combine.'

q: You implemented the same kind of agent in Loop 5 (LangChain chain) and Loop 6 (LangGraph). Most production agent codebases use LangGraph or similar. Why?
answer_outline: Three production reasons. (1) Real agents have branching — different tools for different inputs, different recovery paths for different errors, parallel sub-tasks. A graph expresses this directly; a chain forces it into nested `RunnableBranch` / `RunnableParallel` compositions that get hard to read. (2) Observability — `graph.stream(updates)` lets you tail an agent run node-by-node, which is the dominant production debugging move. Chain callbacks give you steps but not a stable graph topology to reason against. (3) Checkpointing — LangGraph's checkpointers (memory, Postgres, etc.) snapshot graph state at every node, enabling pause/resume, time-travel debugging, and human-in-the-loop interrupts. None of that is straightforward in a chain. The trade-off: more ceremony for trivial agents. Use a chain when the flow is genuinely linear; use a graph the moment branching appears, because retrofitting is expensive.
